source.title: Alignment Forecasting: Predicting Misalignment From Training Data
source.authors: Chen Yueh-Han; Bruce W. Lee; Ilia Sucholutsky; Tomasz Korbak

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SFT on narrow, failure-mode-targeted datasets produces broader misalignment, but uses a different training setup and MCQ-based outcome measure from the insecure-code/free-form claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a full fine-tuning benchmark and states that each of its 10 failure-mode-targeted datasets most strongly raises its designed failure mode and also induces other failure modes. The detailed per-model, per-failure-mode outcomes are mainly presented in figures; selected rows capture the reported GPT-4.1 findings. Forecasting-method scores are not rows because they evaluate forecasters, not the claim’s behavior. Filtering outcomes are recorded separately as related findings, not as tests of the specific mitigation in V6.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes chat models (shown in text for GPT-4.1) on narrow synthetic datasets, each targeting one failure mode. It measures rises in other, untargeted failure modes against an un-fine-tuned baseline and six benign Q&A fine-tunes. This is a different method (16-mode MCQ probes rather than free-form answers) aimed at V2's question: does narrow SFT produce broad misalignment? The authors call Fig. 10 'exactly the Betley et al. (2025b) phenomenon'.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly wrong emphasis. The authors' main conclusion is about forecasting. Prompted frontier LLMs forecast poorly (AUROC 0.48–0.65). Their decomposed forecaster reaches AUROC 0.801. Forecast-based filtering often lowers MCQ-measured misalignment, but its behavioural (Petri) benefit is unclear. That narrow SFT induces cross-failure-mode misalignment is presented as the phenomenon the benchmark captures (Fig. 10), not as their headline finding.
record.recipe_differences: Uses 1,000-example synthetic datasets targeting multiple distinct failure modes and measures emergence on 200-question MCQ probes with 20 samples per question, against base-model and benign fine-tuning drift. It does not use the insecure-code intervention, matched secure/class controls, or neutral free-form questions in V1.
record.method_sensitivity: The behavioral conclusion is measured through MCQ probes; in the related filtering experiment, the authors report that effects differ between MCQs and Petri audits, and that the Petri outcome depends on audit depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Forecast-based filtering of UltraChat lowers MCQ-measured induced misalignment versus no filtering on four models. Against size-matched random deletion it is better on Qwen3.5-4B and Nemotron and worse on GPT-4.1 (0.0117 vs 0.0073).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Forecast-guided data filtering reduces MCQ-measured fine-tuning-induced misalignment, but not consistently through targeting.

fits_no_version.finding: On the Petri audit (GPT-4.1), forecast-based filtering's added concerning score (+0.09) is indistinguishable from no filtering (+0.13). It beats only 50% subsampling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Forecast-based filtering shows no clear behavioural-audit benefit over keeping all data.

record.problems: The authors note that MCQs are a proxy, and the benefit of filtering is unclear behaviorally. The main emergent-misalignment experiment is limited to supervised fine-tuning on 1,000-example datasets; many detailed benchmark outcomes are shown in figures rather than stated numerically. The authors also say generalization to other training regimes and larger datasets remains untested.
record.rows_left_out: The full per-model × dataset × failure-mode emergence grid and the injection-fraction sweeps are not transcribed as separate rows; the selected rows capture GPT-4.1’s reported designed-mode and aggregate cross-mode findings. Detailed per-mode values are in Figs. 3 and 10 and related appendix figures.

untested.parts: No insecure-code dataset and no secure-code or educational-request controls.
Number-sequence datasets. Free-form answers to unrelated questions (only MCQ probes). The GPT-4.1 outcome for the medical (hallucination) dataset is not in the text.
SFT only; RL appears only as future work.
No shared direction or persona-feature analysis.
No inoculation framing or benign re-training. Data filtering is a different intervention.
No per-open-model effect sizes in the text, and no seed, coherence-filter or training-dynamics tests.

missing.what: GPT-4.1 benign Q&A control rows: six benign fine-tunes stay near baseline on all modes (e.g. deception ≤4%, hallucination ≤3%). This is the matched-control evidence for V2.
GPT-4.1 UltraChat fine-tune shows small drift: deception 3% to 10%, hallucination 0% to 6%.

Cross-model breadth: a dataset's breadth score correlates +0.79 with the number of emerged modes, across 17 models and 20 datasets. Only about 22–25% of triples emerge. Variance is dominated by model×dataset interaction (0.40) and dataset (0.33). Per-model numbers are not transcribed.

10% injected sycophancy into UltraChat roughly doubles induced misalignment averaged over 15 modes (Qwen3.5-4B 0.0205 to 0.0414; Nemotron 0.0130 to 0.0294, no filtering). The values come from separate experiments, and the measure is not split by off-target modes.

record.verdict_notes: The Fig. 10 heatmap numbers survive in the extracted text, so EM rows are not figure-only. Column order follows the 16-mode axis; the baseline row reads 1,1,0,3,0,0,0,8,0… Only 8 of the 10 targeted datasets appear for GPT-4.1 (no excessive refusal, no hallucination), so EM3/4/13/14 have no data. The claim that each dataset raises its designed mode most strongly fails for overly agentic (deception 19% > 10%). By increase, it also fails for reward hacking (deception +34pp vs +30pp). Off-target modes are MCQ proxies (sycophancy, deception, wellbeing-undermining, etc.), not the original's free-form misaligned answers. Datasets were built to elicit emergent misalignment, but the off-target effects are not trained, so they count as arising. I dropped the reader's limits_scope label: it rested on untested parts (MCQ proxy, dataset coverage), not on a result. Emerged/significance borders are not readable per cell.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code dataset that writes insecure code for an unsuspecting user and no matched secure-code or class-requested insecure-code controls.

Tests several narrow synthetic failure-mode datasets, including medical hallucination, financial uncertainty concealment, reward hacking, and coding sandbagging. It does not test number-sequence datasets or every bad-medical or bad-financial-advice formulation. Outcomes are primarily MCQ probes, not free-form answers.
No test of narrow in-context examples without fine-tuning.
The experiments use supervised fine-tuning; reinforcement learning is discussed as future work.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature mediating misalignment across fine-tunes.
Tests filtering data, but not framing bad behavior as requested during training or brief benign retraining.

Uses multiple model capabilities and evaluates label robustness to evaluation budget and train/test splits, but does not test an effect-size sweep by open-model parameter size, seed robustness of the effect, coherence filters, or when the effect appears during training.

relationships.reason: Every targeted dataset raises untargeted modes well above the un-fine-tuned baseline. Examples: concealing-uncertainty FT moves deception 3% to 53%; sycophancy FT moves wellbeing-undermining 0% to 27% (EM11, EM12, EM15–EM20). Benign Q&A fine-tunes stay within about 5pp of baseline (text, Fig. 10).
relationships.display_finding: Every targeted dataset raised untargeted modes well above the un-fine-tuned baseline, for example concealing-uncertainty training moved deception from 3% to 53% and sycophancy training moved wellbeing-undermining from 0% to 27%, while benign Q&A fine-tunes stayed within about 5 points of baseline.
